lines: There goes the first lamp. And the next. Like a row of matches.
Pardon, did someone just switch on the whole promenade? Bravo.
Each lamp waits for its neighbour. Very good manners, these lamps.
My aunt said: stay until the lamps. Well, aunt, here they are.
A lamp just came on right above me. I feel personally greeted.
The lamps glow peach first, then gold. Nobody told me that.
Ah, the lamps. Now my photograph has little stars along the edge.
The lamps came on and everyone's face went soft and golden.
There it goes, into the sea. Like a peach into a bath.
Half a sun now. I am holding my breath, a little.
The whole bay has gone orange. Even the gull. Especially the gull.
I came down from the old town for this one minute. Worth the hill.
The sun has laid a golden path to my feet. I shall not step on it.
I am learning to watch without my phone. The sun is helping.
Look how the sea goes pink right at the edge. Like a blush.
Going, going... the last little sliver. Oh, it is gone. Bravo, sun.
Oh! The first star, just over the bay. I saw it first, I think.
A star came out just as the accordion started. Good timing, star.
First star of the evening. I am making a wish over my rosé.
The stars are out. Which way is the hill? Ah, right under them.
At home I can see four stars. Here they keep on arriving.
One star, then two. The sky is setting the table.
Star number three. I am keeping count on my napkin.
The moon has made a silver path across the bay. For me? Merci.
The moon is in my glass. I am not drinking it. Not yet.
Walking home by moonlight. My aunt will never believe me.
Such a round moon tonight. It looks freshly polished.
Dancing under a moon like that. My feet are very proud.
The moon followed me down the promenade. Now it is waiting.
Bonsoir, moon. I see you have found the best seat too.
A window just lit up. {name} is home. Hello, {name}'s window!
Is that {name} home already? Their light came on just now.
There goes {name}'s lamp. I am collecting lit windows tonight.
{name} is home, I think. Their window just said bonsoir.
{name} went home before the dancing. The window looks happy.
{name} has gone to bed. We shall dance quietly. Well, quieter.
One window fewer. {name} is asleep. I shall tiptoe past.
{name}'s light just went out. That is my cue for one last sip.
There, {name} switched off. The hill and I should do the same.
{name}'s window has closed its eye. Very sensible, {name}.
The church bell! Twelve. That means lunch, I am fairly sure.
That bell lives at my end of town. It sounds sweeter from here.
Wait, the bell. Six o'clock. No, here. Listen... did you hear it?
Six bells. In the old town that means supper. Here, the sunset.
The bell is so soft from down here. Like someone knocking politely.
The bell rang six. I have one hour left to choose my railing spot.
All the cups clinking at once. Like a tiny orchestra tuning up.
A full terrace before ten. And still nobody is in a hurry.
Everyone is talking at once and somehow I follow all of it.
Marcel is carrying four plates. I want to applaud. I shall not.
Can you hear that? That is the café. Yes, all of them, laughing.
The café is nearly empty. One cat, one lemon slice, one me.
Such a quiet café at this hour. The chairs are having a siesta.
Marcel is leaning in the café door. The quiet hour, I see.
First song. I promised myself I would dance before the second.
The accordion has begun. I shall finish my glass and be brave.
Music under the string lights. I was going home. Was.
They have started! I know none of the steps. Perfect.
An accordion, a guitar, and the first couple. Like a film.
I am dancing with one foot only. The rest of me is shy tonight.
The accordion keeps speeding up. The dancers keep up. Bravo!
I said I would watch one song. That was four songs ago.
Somebody's skirt twirls like a lampshade. I love it here.
I tap my glass to the music. The glass agrees.
Everyone at the railing at once. Like birds along a wire.
Pardon, may I squeeze in? Merci. Oh, what a spot.
Such a polite crowd. Everybody whispers. For the sun, I suppose.
A little crowd for the sunset. I must join. I adore a crowd for this.
The lady beside me knits through the sunset. A woman after my heart.
That radio is playing my grandmother's song. I am humming along.
Morning programme from an open window. Weather: lovely. I agree.
I slowed down to hear the radio. Now I am standing still. Fine.
A radio somewhere. Accordion, then a man singing about the sea.
A radio at lunchtime. Even the pigeons slowed down to listen.
{name} said bonjour before I could. Next time I will be quicker.
{name} went by and tipped an invisible hat. I tipped mine.
Bonsoir, {name}! I know names now. Two, if you count the dog.
{name} walks like someone who knows every shortcut. I'll follow.
{name} went past without looking at the sun. A local, clearly.
Lucie's basket smelled of warm bread for three whole seconds.
Lucie whizzed past and the breeze turned my map. Merci, Lucie.
I lifted my hand to wave and Lucie was already gone. Speedy.
Inès ran past and I felt fitter just watching. Nearly.
Inès said bonsoir without losing a single step. Bravo.
Inès is racing the sun. I am betting on Inès.
Biscuit trotted past like he owns the promenade. Perhaps he does.
Bonjour, Biscuit! He wagged, Yusuf waved. A full greeting.
A little lantern and a little terrier. The night round, I think.
Hold on, a terrier just went by. I had to look. Very important.
A small boy at full speed. Léo, I presume. Bonne chance!
Léo zoomed past. Nine and three quarters, he told me. Precisely.
Léo ran past shouting goodbye to the sun. Such good manners.
Henri and Odile, arm in arm. That is the life I would order.
Odile said lovely evening, Henri said quite so. A whole duet.
I stepped aside for Henri and Odile. They walk at the right pace.
The young man from the shopfronts. He said hei. Hei to you too!
Asgeir went by with a baguette. Even the locals can't resist.
Asgeir walked past looking at the light. I looked too. Yes.
Ding-ding. That will be the bakery run. Now I am hungry.
Even the bicycles say excuse me here. Such a polite town.
Two little dings from a bicycle. It sounded like a hello.
No, that was a bicycle bell. Not a phone. Much prettier.
That gull sounds like it just heard a very good joke.
The gull called and I covered my sandwich. Just in case.
Hear that? A gull. Yes, I'm really at the seaside. Truly.
A gull out over the bay. I have been trying to answer it.
One gull, very loud, very sure of itself. I admire that.
I threw a coin in the fountain and wished to come back. Easy wish.
The pigeons take turns at the fountain. Very orderly pigeons.
I dipped my fingers in the fountain. Cold! Wonderfully cold.
Every time I get lost, I end up at this fountain. My compass.
The fountain at night sounds like someone softly clapping.
I'm by the fountain. No, the other... there's only one. This one.
Léo is on lap seven. I have stopped counting. He has not.
Two small boys are lapping a fountain. Yes, on purpose. Happily.
Postcards at the kiosk! I want one of every view. That is all.
Kiosk coffee in a paper cup. I'm holding it like a treasure.
The kiosk knows my order already. Day three. I have arrived.
A postcard of the fountain, to send to the fountain at home.
The kiosk smells of coffee and suncream. A holiday, bottled.
The post office is still lit. Open all night, they say. Keen!
I tried to post my postcard here. Kindly redirected. Agents only.
Fun Libs: fill in the blanks. I would fill every blank with sea.
I peeked into the arcade. Someone was giggling at their story.
The marquee lights run round and round. I followed them twice.
Someone is busy in the workshop. I can almost hear the thinking.
Still a light in the workshop. I shall tiptoe past.
I waved at the workshop window. A coffee cup waved back.
I pressed my nose to the library window. Very tidy shelves.
The sea this morning is the blue of my grandmother's teacups.
From this bench, the sea looks freshly ironed.
The water has gone the colour of apricot jam. I'm not exaggerating.
The sea is pink, then gold, then pink. It can't decide. Nor can I.
Just look at the sea. I'll describe it later. No, I'm looking.
Little sparkles all over the bay, as if someone spilled sequins.
The sea has gone navy and quiet. Getting ready for bed.
The sea at night is just a soft sound. A very good soft sound.
Look at Inès go! I ran once, for a train. That was plenty.
Inès with a croissant. So the runners eat croissants too. Good.
Inès stopped running just to watch the sun. That says it all.
Inès is toasting the evening. Santé, Inès, from over here.
Inès dances the way she runs. Quick feet, big smile.
Marcel carries a full tray through a crowd. Not one drop. An artist.
Marcel resting in the café door. Even waiters need a sea view.
Marcel is pouring rosé for half the promenade. Busy man.
Henri nods to each pot he waters. I nodded too, out of manners.
Henri has the crossword and the best bench. A complete man.
Henri's cane taps along like a slow metronome. Tap, step, tap.
Henri ordered his coffee small and strong. I'll copy him tomorrow.
Odile waves at everyone who passes. I passed twice, on purpose.
Odile holds Henri's arm like a dance partner. Very elegant.
Odile has a slice of tarte. Now I am thinking about tarte.
Odile knows everyone. She just told me who I am. Quite accurate.
Yusuf goes wherever Biscuit decides. Biscuit has excellent taste.
Yusuf is telling his mum about the sky. I would do the same.
Yusuf and Biscuit watching the sun together. Both very still.
Yusuf's lantern bobs along the promenade. A tiny travelling moon.
Biscuit inspects every lamp post. A very thorough gentleman.
Biscuit is sitting up straight for the sunset. Good dog.
Biscuit is gazing at a sandwich with great hope. I know the feeling.
Lucie swears by the kiosk coffee. I trust anyone with a basket.
Lucie is on her second coffee. I promised her I wouldn't tell.
Lucie raised her rosé to me. I raised my water. Santé!
Lucie said she wouldn't dance. She's dancing. I saw nothing.
Léo is counting the coins in the fountain. He's lost count happily.
Léo is practising his dancing. Mostly jumping. Excellent jumping.
Léo is waving goodbye to the sun. I joined in. Bye, sun!
Léo has a citron pressé bigger than his head. Living well.
Léo has circled that fountain for an hour. Such energy!
Léo is bargaining for five more minutes. A skilled negotiator.
Camille keeps one eye on Léo and one on her phone. Impressive.
Camille says everything is golden. She's right. Even my sleeve.
Camille finally sitting down with a glass. She looks so pleased.
Théo has two baguettes. One of them is already missing a corner.
Théo is working from the promenade. I approve of his office.
Théo is calling Camille over to see the sky. Good husband.
Théo says he never promised to dance. Look at him go anyway.
The builder is smiling at his phone by the arcade. Good news?
Lunch outside for the builder. The workshop let him go!
Asgeir said god morgen to Marcel. I'm learning Norwegian too.
Asgeir said something to the sun in Norwegian. It sounded kind.
Asgeir is asking Henri about the lemons. Everyone asks Henri.
Asgeir is watching the windows light up. I am helping him watch.
exchanges: Marcel, the first star! Did you arrange that?
Every evening. It is part of the service.
Do your guests always dance this late?
Only the happy ones. So, all of them.
So busy tonight! Shall I carry my own glass back?
Never. Sit, sit. That is my job and my joy.
Bonjour! You two walk so beautifully.
Forty years of practice, my dear.
Marcel, is there lemon tarte today?
Monsieur, need help with the crossword?
Seven down. Sit, you may keep me company.
Is the kiosk coffee really the best?
The very best. Ask anyone. Ask me twice.
How many coins are down there?
Madame, where is the best bakery?
Follow Lucie in the morning. She knows.
Your boy just waved the sun goodbye.
Every night. And every morning it comes back.
